corrected_value.title: Interinstitutional variation in emerging adulthood: Does selectivity matter?

decisions.quote:
Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) reduced 20 of the

markers of adulthood identified by Arnett (1994; 1997) into four theoretically derived

dimensions (Role Transitions, Norm Compliance, Relational Maturity, and Independence)

following previous work (Badger, Nelson, & Barry, 2006; Nelson, Padilla-Walker, Carroll,

Madsen, Barry, & Badger, 2007; also see Fosse, Grahe, & Reifman, 2016). Because Faas et al.

(this issue) examine the psychometric properties of these items, and because our question is

confirmatory rather than exploratory, we employed the constructs used by Fosse and Toyokawa

(2016).
decisions.location: Introduction - Overview of Fosse and Toyokawa (lines 156-170); References (lines 1173-1180)
decisions.reason: The shipped row misattributed the tested original to a same-first-author, same-year sibling reference in the bibliography—Fosse, Grahe, & Reifman (2016), 'Markers of Adulthood Subscale Development: Comparative Review and Assessment of Inductive and Deductive Psychometrics'—which is cited only as background psychometric work on the four subscale dimensions (lines 164, 182). Both the paper's title/text and the shipped row's own outcome_quote show that this row represents the primary close replication of Fosse, N. E., & Toyokawa, T. (2016), 'Interinstitutional variation in emerging adulthood: Does selectivity matter?', matching blind target 0.

decisions.quote:
As a close replication of Fosse and Toyokawa (2016), the present

findings supported our pre-registered hypotheses that liberal arts status predicted decreased

perceived importance and lower attainment of some constructs of Markers of Adulthood, but did

not support predictions that selectivity would also predict such differences.
decisions.reason: With the dependent original identity resolved to Fosse and Toyokawa (2016), both the Abstract and Discussion explicitly report partial support ('mixed'): the pre-registered hypotheses for liberal arts status predicting lower perceived importance (Hypothesis 2) and lower Relational Maturity achievement (part of Hypothesis 4) were supported, whereas the planned linear predictions for institutional selectivity (Hypotheses 1 and 3) were not supported. Statistical power is discussed in the Limitations section as a caveat for future multi-site studies, not as a verdict that the replication is uninformative.

decisions.quote:
As a close replication of Fosse and Toyokawa (2016), the present

findings supported our pre-registered hypotheses that liberal arts status predicted decreased

perceived importance and lower attainment of some constructs of Markers of Adulthood, but did

not support predictions that selectivity would also predict such differences. Our findings provide

further evidence of the institutional effects that emerge in multi-sample individual difference

studies and extends those findings with a broader and more diverse sample than was considered

previously.
decisions.reason: The study collected new survey data from an independent multi-institution sample (EAMMi2, 2016 data) to re-test the published findings of Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) (which used 2004 EAMMI data), making it a replication.

corrected_value.authors: Badger, S., Nelson, L. J., & Barry, C. M.
corrected_value.title: Perceptions of the transition to adulthood among Chinese and American emerging adults.

decisions.location: Discussion - Summary of Findings and Institutional Characteristics and Emerging Adulthood (lines 781-815); Results - Demographic Controls (lines 590-618, Table 4); References (lines 1121-1125)
decisions.quote:
Additionally, women rated Normative Compliance and Relational Maturity as more

important indicators of adulthood, and they reported higher achievement of Normative

Compliance. This result supports prior findings of higher ratings of importance for Normative

Compliance items for women among both American and Chinese participants, though no other

sex differences were reported (Badger et al., 2006). Other research also documented women

rating Normative Compliance as more important than men did, though they also found women

rated other constructs as important for this transition (Nelson et al., 2007). The lack of difference

in achievement in our sample is a curious finding that should be further considered, but the

pattern of perceived importance seems consistent with prior literature.

Institutional Characteristics and Emerging Adulthood

       Although replication of these age and gender effects are important, it was the replication

of associations with institutional selectivity and liberal arts status that represented our primary

questions. Specifically, we replicated Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) who first examined these

variables.
decisions.reason: Using independent multi-site survey data from EAMMi2 (N = 1,572 students across 23 institutions), the authors empirically tested age and gender fixed effects across all four Markers of Adulthood importance and achievement subscales in Results ('Demographic Controls', lines 590-618, Table 4) and explicitly state in the Discussion that they 'replicated previously observed age and gender differences in markers of adulthood (Badger et al., 2006, Nelson et al., 2007)' (lines 781-782) and refer to the 'replication of these age and gender effects' (line 809). They directly compare their gender results (women rating Normative Compliance and Relational Maturity as more important and reporting higher Normative Compliance achievement) to Badger, S., Nelson, L. J., & Barry, C. M. (2006), 'Perceptions of the transition to adulthood among Chinese and American emerging adults', International Journal of Behavioral Development, 30(1), 84-93, doi:10.1177/0165025406062128, which reported higher female importance ratings for Normative Compliance among Chinese and American emerging adults with no other sex differences. Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) is not an intermediary replication chain for these effects because it treated biological sex and age only as covariates when testing institutional selectivity and liberal arts status (lines 186-190, 809-817). The only shipped row (input_row_index 2425, originally citing the psychometric manuscript Fosse, Grahe, & Reifman, 2016, and source-adjudicated to target_index 0, Fosse & Toyokawa, 2016) and sibling target_index 2 (Nelson et al., 2007, a separate Journal of Family Psychology study of emerging adults and their parents) are distinct works, so report equivalence does not apply. Note: prior_state_path was absent in the frozen snapshot and prior_adjudication_path adjudicated only input_row_index 2425 (target_index 0).

important indicators of adulthood, and they reported higher achievement of Normative

Institutional Characteristics and Emerging Adulthood

       Although replication of these age and gender effects are important, it was the replication

decisions.reason: In Results ('Demographic Controls', lines 590-618, Table 4), the authors test age and gender differences across the four Markers of Adulthood importance and achievement subscales in their new EAMMi2 sample (N = 1,572), and in the Discussion they explicitly state that they 'replicated previously observed age and gender differences in markers of adulthood (Badger et al., 2006, Nelson et al., 2007)' (lines 781-782) and refer to the 'replication of these age and gender effects' (line 809). They directly compare their observed gender differences (women rating Normative Compliance and Relational Maturity as more important than men) against Nelson, L. J., Padilla-Walker, L. M., Carroll, J. S., Madsen, S. D., Barry, C. M., & Badger, S. (2007), '“If you want me to treat you like an adult, start acting like one!” Comparing the criteria that emerging adults and their parents have for adulthood', Journal of Family Psychology, 21(4), 665-674 (no DOI printed in source), which found that women rated Normative Compliance as well as other constructs as more important than men did. Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) is not an intermediary in a replication chain for these age/gender findings because it only controlled for biological sex and age while testing institutional selectivity and liberal arts status (lines 186-190, 809-817). This 2007 Journal of Family Psychology study of emerging adults and their parents is an independent original study distinct from the only shipped row (input_row_index 2425, originally citing Fosse, Grahe, & Reifman, 2016, and source-adjudicated to target_index 0, Fosse & Toyokawa, 2016) and from sibling target_index 1 (Badger et al., 2006, a 2006 International Journal of Behavioral Development cross-cultural study of Chinese and American emerging adults). Note: prior_state_path was absent in the frozen snapshot and prior_adjudication_path adjudicated only input_row_index 2425 (target_index 0).
